lessons.why: The PC speaker needs only the PIT, so it is a quick first sound before you tackle a real audio device.
objectives: After this lesson you can drive the PC speaker at a chosen frequency.
After this lesson you can explain sample rate, bit depth and DMA buffers for real sound cards.
lessons.checkpoint: Play a short tune through the PC speaker in QEMU (-audiodev with -machine pcspk-audiodev).

lessons.title: PCM audio with AC97
lessons.why: Real audio means streaming sample buffers with DMA and refilling them on interrupt. AC97 is simple and emulated by QEMU and VirtualBox.
objectives: After this lesson you can find the AC97 controller on PCI and reset the codec.
After this lesson you can build a buffer descriptor list and refill buffers on interrupt.
After this lesson you can parse a WAV header and convert its format if needed.
lessons.checkpoint: Play a WAV file from your filesystem through QEMU's -device AC97 without gaps.

lessons.title: Intel High Definition Audio
lessons.why: HD Audio is what real machines have. The controller is a DMA engine, and the work is in talking to codecs and finding a path from a converter to a speaker.
objectives: After this lesson you can set up the CORB and RIRB rings and send verbs to a codec.
After this lesson you can walk the codec's widget graph from a DAC to an output pin.
After this lesson you can stream PCM through a buffer descriptor list.
lessons.checkpoint: Under QEMU's -device intel-hda -device hda-duplex, list every widget of the codec with its type, then play the same WAV file as in the AC97 lesson.

tracks.title: Elective: Networking
tracks.summary: A layered stack design, a NIC driver, ARP, IP and ICMP, real-hardware NICs and the scope of TLS.
tracks.goal: Send and receive Ethernet frames, answer a ping from the host, and judge what a TLS client would still need.

modules.title: A minimal stack
modules.summary: Design, driver, and the first protocol that proves it all works.

lessons.title: Network stack design
lessons.why: A network stack is layered. Designing the buffers and layers before writing a driver avoids a rewrite.
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the path of a packet from NIC to socket.
After this lesson you can design packet buffers that move between layers without copying.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a one-page design: driver interface, packet buffer, Ethernet, ARP, IPv4, ICMP, UDP, with what each layer passes on.

lessons.title: A network card driver
lessons.why: QEMU emulates the RTL8139 and Intel e1000. A driver for either gets packets moving.
objectives: After this lesson you can initialise the NIC, set up receive and transmit buffers and read the MAC address.
After this lesson you can send and receive raw Ethernet frames using interrupts.
lessons.checkpoint: Send a broadcast frame from your OS and capture it on the host with QEMU's -object filter-dump and Wireshark.

lessons.title: ARP, IP and ICMP: answer a ping
lessons.why: Replying to ping proves every layer of a minimal stack works.
objectives: After this lesson you can answer ARP requests and keep an ARP cache.
After this lesson you can parse and build IPv4 and ICMP echo packets with correct checksums.
lessons.checkpoint: With -netdev tap (or bridge), ping your OS's IP from the host and get replies. With -netdev user, which cannot deliver host-to-guest ICMP, send an ARP request for 10.0.2.2, then an ICMP echo to it, and print the reply's sequence number and round-trip ticks.

modules.title: Further out
modules.summary: Real NICs and secure connections.

lessons.title: Network cards on real hardware: RTL8169 and Intel i217
lessons.why: QEMU's RTL8139 and e1000 are rare in real machines. The RTL8169 family and Intel's i217 are common in desktops and laptops, and their descriptor rings follow the pattern you already know.
objectives: After this lesson you can compare the descriptor ring designs of the RTL8169 and i217 with the driver you wrote.
After this lesson you can plan a driver for the NIC in a machine you own, starting from its PCI IDs.
lessons.checkpoint: Find your own machine's NIC vendor and device ID (lspci -nn on Linux), decide which article applies, and list how its receive and transmit setup differs from your QEMU driver. If you have the hardware, boot from USB and log a link-up interrupt.

lessons.title: Secure connections: TLS
lessons.why: Most of today's internet needs TLS. It is a large, security-critical project; read it to understand the scope before deciding to port a library instead.
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the TLS 1.3 handshake step by step.
After this lesson you can list what your OS needs first: TCP, a good random source, and time.
After this lesson you can build an entropy pool from RDRAND or TSC jitter and verify a CRC32 routine against a known-good implementation.
lessons.checkpoint: Implement the entropy source described in Random Number Generator: RDRAND if CPUID reports it, otherwise TSC jitter mixed into a pool. Add a CRC32 routine and check it against the host's output on a 1 MB file. Then write down every other prerequisite your OS is missing for a TLS client, and record the write-or-port decision in DECISIONS.md.

tracks.title: Elective: Porting Software and Self-Hosting
tracks.summary: A toolchain that knows your OS, a ported libc, C++ and Rust support, real programs, and the road to compiling your OS on itself.
tracks.goal: Build programs with your own OS-specific GCC, port a libc and real software, and reach the first self-hosting milestone.

modules.title: Toolchain and libraries
modules.summary: Your libc goes into the sysroot first, then a compiler that targets your OS.

lessons.title: A toolchain that targets your OS
lessons.why: A compiler that knows your OS (i686-myos-gcc) builds user programs without hand-written flags and is the first step to porting software. Your libc from the core path must be installed in the sysroot first: libgcc needs at least its headers.
objectives: After this lesson you can add your OS as a target to binutils and GCC.
After this lesson you can build user programs with your OS's own triplet.
lessons.checkpoint: Build a hello-world user program with your own i686-myos-gcc, using the libc headers and crt0 already in your sysroot, and run it on your OS.

lessons.title: Port Newlib
lessons.why: A ported libc gives you most of the C standard library at once, so more software builds without changes.
objectives: After this lesson you can add your OS to Newlib and write the system call glue it needs.
After this lesson you can build user programs against Newlib with your OS toolchain.
lessons.checkpoint: Run a program using fopen, fprintf and qsort from Newlib on your OS.

lessons.title: C++ in the kernel and in user space
further: C++ to ASM linkage in GCC
lessons.why: C++ works in a kernel once you provide what its runtime expects: global constructors, new and delete, and either no exceptions and RTTI or the support code for them.
objectives: After this lesson you can list the runtime support C++ needs: constructors, operator new and delete, __cxa_pure_virtual and guard functions.
After this lesson you can build kernel C++ with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti and say what you give up.
After this lesson you can decide whether user programs get exceptions, and what porting libsupc++ involves.
lessons.checkpoint: Add one C++ file to your kernel with a global object whose constructor prints a line; it must print before kernel_main's first message. A pure virtual call must reach your panic, not a random address.

modules.title: Real programs
modules.summary: Port software, then aim at self-hosting.

lessons.title: Port existing software
lessons.why: Porting real programs shows exactly which system calls and libc functions are missing, faster than any checklist.
objectives: After this lesson you can configure an autotools project for your OS target with a sysroot.
After this lesson you can list missing functions from link errors and implement or stub them.
lessons.checkpoint: Cross-compile one small real program (a text editor or a scripting language) for your OS and run it.

lessons.title: Porting the Rust standard library
lessons.why: Rust programs expect std. Porting it to your OS gives you a second language for user space and shows exactly which system interfaces a modern runtime calls.
objectives: After this lesson you can explain how Rust's std is organised per target and what a new OS target must supply.
After this lesson you can add a target for your OS and build std on top of your libc.
lessons.checkpoint: Build a Rust hello-world that uses std for your OS target and run it on your OS.

lessons.title: Toward self-hosting: GCC and Python on your OS
lessons.why: Compiling your OS under your OS is the traditional finish line. It is a multi-week project: the time shown covers the reading and the first milestone, binutils running on your OS.
objectives: After this lesson you can list the OS features a compiler needs: spawn or fork/exec, files, pipes and enough memory.
After this lesson you can build a program for your OS as a Canadian cross.
After this lesson you can plan the milestones from binutils to a native GCC to rebuilding your own kernel.
lessons.checkpoint: First milestone: build binutils as a Canadian cross for your OS and run as --version and ld --version on it. Write the remaining milestones (native GCC, Python, rebuilding your kernel) in DECISIONS.md with the system calls each one still needs.

tracks.title: Elective: Beyond i686: 64-bit, UEFI, ARM and RISC-V
tracks.summary: A planned port of your kernel to x86-64, booting through your own UEFI loader, and second architectures.
tracks.goal: Run your kernel's test suite on x86-64, boot a kernel through your own UEFI loader, and print from kernels on AArch64 and RISC-V.

modules.title: Port to x86-64
modules.summary: Move the kernel you already have to long mode as a planned port, with the test suite as your guide.

lessons.title: x86-64 and long mode
lessons.why: Nearly all current PCs run 64-bit kernels. Long mode changes registers, paging depth, the calling convention and the system call path. Treat what follows as a port of your kernel over several sittings, not a single switch.
objectives: After this lesson you can list what changes in long mode compared to protected mode.
After this lesson you can describe 4-level paging and canonical addresses.
After this lesson you can explain the x86-64 System V calling convention.
lessons.checkpoint: Write the steps (CPUID check, PAE, page tables, EFER.LME, PG, far jump) from protected mode to long mode, with the register and bit for each.

lessons.title: Optional route: set up long mode by hand
further: Creating a 64-bit kernel using a separate loader
QEMU and GDB in long mode
lessons.why: Doing the switch yourself once makes every 64-bit bootloader's handover understandable.
objectives: After this lesson you can build identity-mapped 4-level page tables in assembly.
After this lesson you can enable long mode and load a 64-bit GDT.
After this lesson you can call 64-bit C code compiled with -mno-red-zone.
lessons.checkpoint: From your Multiboot entry, switch to long mode and call a 64-bit kernel_main that prints "64-bit" on qemu-system-x86_64.

lessons.title: A 64-bit kernel with Limine
lessons.why: Limine hands you long mode, a higher-half mapping, a framebuffer and a memory map. It is a practical base for a 64-bit port of your kernel. If you did the previous lesson you can keep your own entry code instead; the rest of this module works with either.
objectives: After this lesson you can build a kernel for the Limine boot protocol.
After this lesson you can use Limine requests for the memory map and framebuffer.
After this lesson you can link with -mcmodel=kernel in the top 2 GiB.
lessons.checkpoint: Boot your kernel through Limine on qemu-system-x86_64, fill the framebuffer with a colour, and print the memory map over serial.

lessons.title: Port the kernel: compiler flags, IDT, ISR stubs and TSS
lessons.why: Most 32-bit C compiles unchanged, but the parts that touch the CPU do not: interrupt gates are 16 bytes, there is no pusha, iret becomes iretq, the TSS holds stack pointers and the IST, and kernel code must not use the red zone.
objectives: After this lesson you can build the kernel with -mno-red-zone, -mcmodel=kernel and a libgcc built to match.
After this lesson you can write 64-bit IDT gates and ISR stubs that push registers one by one and return with iretq.
After this lesson you can set up a 64-bit TSS with an IST stack for double faults.
lessons.checkpoint: Your make test suite passes on qemu-system-x86_64: the divide-by-zero, ud2, SSP and kprintf tests print the same results as the 32-bit build. Set IST1 on vector 8, mark the #GP gate not present, and execute an instruction that raises #GP (load a bad selector into DS): the #DF handler must run and report an RSP inside the IST1 stack instead of the machine triple-faulting.

lessons.title: 4-level paging, the higher half and debugging in long mode
articles: QEMU and GDB in long mode
lessons.why: Your map_page and frame allocator assumed two levels. Long mode uses four, with canonical addresses and the NX bit, and Limine hands you a higher-half direct map to build on. GDB also needs a workaround when the CPU changes mode under it. In Paging, read §64-Bit Paging and §Page Map Table Entries this time.
objectives: After this lesson you can walk and edit PML4, PDPT, PD and PT entries, including the NX bit.
After this lesson you can reach physical memory through the bootloader's higher-half direct map.
After this lesson you can debug a long-mode kernel in GDB despite the mode switch.
lessons.checkpoint: Your map/unmap harness tests pass on x86-64: map a frame at a free kernel address in the top half, write, unmap, and get a page fault with the right CR2. Break in the page-fault handler with GDB and print the faulting address. Then allocate a kernel stack with an unmapped guard page below it, overflow it, and confirm the #DF handler runs on IST1.

lessons.title: SYSCALL, SWAPGS and the 64-bit user boundary
lessons.why: In 64-bit kernels the fast system call path and per-CPU data via GS replace int 0x80 and global variables. Errors here are security holes.
objectives: After this lesson you can configure STAR, LSTAR and SFMASK for SYSCALL.
After this lesson you can use SWAPGS to reach per-CPU kernel data.
After this lesson you can return to user mode with SYSRET safely.
lessons.checkpoint: A 64-bit user program calls write and exit through SYSCALL; GS-based per-CPU data holds the kernel stack pointer.

modules.title: UEFI
modules.summary: What UEFI changes, a UEFI application, and your own loader.

lessons.title: What UEFI changes
lessons.why: New PCs boot UEFI, not BIOS. UEFI gives you a richer environment before your kernel and different rules after it.
objectives: After this lesson you can explain boot services versus runtime services.
After this lesson you can describe the EFI System Partition and GPT.
After this lesson you can run QEMU with OVMF firmware.
lessons.checkpoint: Boot QEMU with OVMF and reach the UEFI shell; list the mapped filesystems.

lessons.title: A UEFI application
lessons.why: A UEFI application is the modern equivalent of the boot sector: the first code of yours the firmware runs.
objectives: After this lesson you can build a PE32+ UEFI application.
After this lesson you can print through the simple text output protocol.
After this lesson you can place BOOTX64.EFI on an ESP image.
After this lesson you can set up a PE32+ toolchain (MinGW-w64, or clang targeting x86_64-windows), or use GNU-EFI's ELF-to-PE conversion.
lessons.checkpoint: OVMF in QEMU runs your BOOTX64.EFI automatically and prints Hello from UEFI.

lessons.title: From UEFI to your kernel
further: Using UEFI Runtime Services in your Kernel
lessons.why: Your own UEFI loader closes the loop on booting: firmware, loader, kernel, all code you understand.
objectives: After this lesson you can read a kernel file from the ESP.
After this lesson you can set a GOP video mode and record the framebuffer.
After this lesson you can get the memory map, exit boot services and jump to the kernel.
lessons.checkpoint: Your UEFI loader loads kernel.elf from the ESP, passes framebuffer and memory map, calls ExitBootServices, and your kernel draws to the screen.

modules.title: Other architectures
modules.summary: Separate the architecture code, then boot on ARM and RISC-V.

lessons.title: Write portable kernel code
articles: Historical Notes on CISC and RISC
lessons.why: Separating architecture code early makes a second port a matter of weeks instead of a rewrite.
objectives: After this lesson you can split your kernel into architecture-specific and generic directories.
After this lesson you can handle endianness and memory-mapped registers portably.
lessons.checkpoint: Move every inline assembly and port I/O call in your kernel behind an arch/ interface, and confirm the x86 build still boots.

lessons.title: ARM and AArch64
lessons.why: ARM runs phones, single-board computers and new laptops. Its exception levels, interrupt controller and boot process differ from x86 in important ways.
objectives: After this lesson you can explain ARM exception levels and how they compare to x86 rings.
After this lesson you can boot a minimal AArch64 kernel on QEMU's virt machine and print to its UART.
lessons.checkpoint: Print 'Hello' over the PL011 UART on qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt, then read the current exception level and print it.

lessons.title: AArch64 exceptions, timer and interrupt controller
lessons.why: On ARM the vector table, the interrupt controller and the timer all differ from x86. Getting a timer tick and a readable exception report is the same first milestone you reached on x86, for the same reasons. The exception vector table at VBAR_EL1 is not covered by the wiki: use the Arm Architecture Reference Manual (D1.10, exception vectors).
objectives: After this lesson you can install an exception vector table at VBAR_EL1 and report synchronous exceptions.
After this lesson you can enable the GIC distributor and CPU interface and take the generic timer interrupt.
lessons.checkpoint: On qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt, a timer interrupt through the GIC prints a tick every second, and a deliberate undefined instruction prints ESR_EL1 and ELR_EL1.

lessons.title: Real hardware: Raspberry Pi
lessons.why: A Raspberry Pi is cheap, common, and a good first real-hardware target, with a serial console for debugging.
objectives: After this lesson you can build a kernel image the Pi firmware will boot.
After this lesson you can use a USB-serial adapter to see kernel output on real hardware.
lessons.checkpoint: Boot your kernel on a Raspberry Pi (or qemu -M raspi3b) and read its output over serial.

lessons.title: RISC-V
articles: RISC-V Meaty Skeleton with QEMU virt board
lessons.why: RISC-V is open, small and well specified, which makes it a clean second architecture to learn.
objectives: After this lesson you can boot a kernel on QEMU's RISC-V virt board through OpenSBI.
After this lesson you can explain machine, supervisor and user modes and SBI calls.
lessons.checkpoint: Port your Meaty Skeleton kernel to qemu-system-riscv64 -M virt and print through the SBI console.

tracks.title: Elective: Design Revisited
tracks.summary: Go back to the decisions you made early, now that you have built the parts: language, kernel model and IPC, and how real systems compare.
tracks.goal: Defend or change each entry in DECISIONS.md from experience, with one working experiment behind each.

modules.title: Revisit your decisions
modules.summary: The language and kernel-model choices, judged with what you know now.

lessons.title: Kernels in other languages: revisit the language decision
lessons.why: C is the default, not a requirement. Rebuilding Bare Bones in another language shows what each language needs from a runtime.
objectives: After this lesson you can list what runtime support a language needs in a freestanding kernel.
After this lesson you can weigh Rust, Zig, Ada and others for kernel work.
After this lesson you can link a non-C kernel with your existing boot stub.
lessons.checkpoint: Rebuild the Bare Bones hello kernel in a second language and boot it in QEMU with the same GRUB ISO setup. Update the language entry in DECISIONS.md with what you learned.

lessons.title: IPC in depth
lessons.why: In a microkernel, IPC speed is the system's speed. These pages cover synchronous messages, copying strategies and RPC.
objectives: After this lesson you can implement synchronous send/receive/reply.
After this lesson you can choose between copying, remapping and shared buffers.
After this lesson you can layer RPC on top of messages.
lessons.checkpoint: Benchmark 10,000 round-trip messages between two processes and report the average cycles per round trip using RDTSC.

lessons.title: Kernel architectures compared
lessons.why: You chose a kernel model before you had built processes, IPC or drivers. Now you have, and can judge the trade-offs from experience.
objectives: After this lesson you can compare monolithic, micro, hybrid and exokernel designs on speed, safety and complexity.
After this lesson you can identify which of your drivers could move to user space.
After this lesson you can update your design with reasons.
lessons.checkpoint: Move one driver (keyboard or serial) into a user-mode process that receives IRQ notifications by IPC, and measure keypress latency against the in-kernel version. Update the kernel-model entry in DECISIONS.md with the measurement.

modules.title: The wider world
modules.summary: Real systems, research and the community.

lessons.title: Learn from real systems
lessons.why: Reading a complete small OS after building your own shows you what you did differently and what you missed.
objectives: After this lesson you can build and boot xv6 in QEMU.
After this lesson you can trace a system call through xv6 or Linux.
After this lesson you can list three ideas to bring back into your kernel.
lessons.checkpoint: Build and boot xv6 in QEMU, trace its fork/exec path, and write a comparison with your own process creation.

lessons.title: Where next: projects, papers and the community
further: You Know Your OS Is Advanced When
lessons.why: Reading other kernels' code and design papers is how you keep improving once tutorials run out.
objectives: After this lesson you can pick one hobby OS and one research paper to study next.
After this lesson you can compare your design with an existing system feature by feature.
lessons.checkpoint: Choose one notable project, read how it handles a feature you have built (scheduler, VFS or memory), and write down one idea to adopt and one to reject.
